Title: From vision to reality: agentic AI at Cisco Live Melbourne
Context: Attendees saw real-time threat detection and autonomous response operating across the Cisco Live network
Full Text:
To learn more about the event, its interactive experiences, and what’s coming next in the fast-changing technology space, we spoke with Nairi Adamian, Cisco’s director of solutions engineering for APJC. Drawing on her 25 years of engineering and leadership experience at Cisco, she also shared her perspective on network transformation and empowering engineers in the agentic AI era.

Thank you, Nairi, and congratulations on a successful Cisco Live Melbourne. What stood out as a key highlight this year?

Thank you, Kevin! Last year, on the same stage, we talked about our vision around platform convergence and unifying network operations. This year, we brought that vision completely to life. In the World of Solutions, customers didn’t just look at slides — they had real, conversational interactions with autonomous AI agents managing the Cisco Live network. Customers could actually have a conversation with the NOC AI agent. They could ask it just about any question about how the Cisco Live network was running in that moment. Experiencing that level of interactive autonomy firsthand generated tremendous excitement.

Those customers, or potential customers, got a deep look into the Network Operations Center (NOC).

The NOC is truly the heartbeat of Cisco Live, and hosting it right inside the Cisco Stand was a major focal point. Attendees got to see live network dashboards powered by Splunk and talk directly with our engineering experts about what it takes to deploy, manage, and secure a network. New this year, visitors could engage directly with our NOC AI Agent to query real-time performance stats and explore the exact equipment powering their event experience. Furthermore, on our daily behind-the-scenes tours in collaboration with Endace, customers experienced a live Agentic SOC powered by Splunk Enterprise Security and Cisco Cloud Control — watching us detect, correlate, and autonomously respond to active threats across live conference traffic in real time. It was a powerful, real-world demonstration of AgenticOps in action.

Sounds like all that resonated with the customers.

Yes, while Cisco Cloud Control is currently available in the U.S., it’s coming to APJC in 2027. So, the APJC customers are looking forward to having it here—and they were especially excited to see it in action.

What are some advantages customers say they are looking forward to from Cloud Control?

In talking with customers, a number of key advantages from Cloud Control came up. The first is around operational simplicity. Our customers want to move beyond science-project AI experimentation to trusted, policy-governed outcomes that eliminate operational silos. With Cisco Cloud Control, customers gain a unified platform powering AgenticOps. That enables intelligent automation and simplified network operations across their entire infrastructure.

Security and resilience are major concerns for them.

Yes, teams today are managing highly complex, multi-vendor hybrid and IT/OT environments. In fact, a recent Cisco study revealed that while 83% of organizations plan to deploy AI agents within the next 12 months, only 13% consider their infrastructure truly AI-ready. That readiness gap is where our engineers focus. We help customers architect, identify, and secure autonomous agents within their environments.

Splunk Enterprise Security was well represented in the World of Solutions.

Yes, that was showcased inside our agentic Security Operations Center (SOC). Attendees saw real-time threat detection and autonomous response operating across the Cisco Live network. Through Splunk’s industry-leading telemetry, security teams could watch malicious traffic get identified, isolated, and neutralized as it happened.

At Cisco Live Melbourne, APJC customers saw just how comprehensive Cisco solutions are.

Our customers are looking for a trusted partner who can deliver networks that are both AI-ready and inherently cyber-resilient. Our approach comes down to three core commitments:

First, operational simplicity. With Cisco Cloud Control and AgenticOps, we eliminate operational silos so teams can move from AI experimentation to trusted, closed-loop outcomes.

Second, security fused into the network. Security can’t be an afterthought; it’s built directly into the fabric with Cisco Live Protect and quantum-safe encryption.

And third, AI-ready infrastructure, built on Cisco Silicon One and next-gen Catalyst hardware to handle massive AI data concurrency. Layer Splunk across that entire footprint, and customers get end-to-end visibility they simply can’t get anywhere else. That is why Cisco stands alone in this transformation."

You’ve been an engineer with Cisco for more than 25 years. You’ve seen a lot of change in that time. What else excites you about the future?

What excites me most over the next 12 months is that engineers are going to have an unprecedented level of technical capability, right at their fingertips — and what they will be able to deliver, at a speed that is simply unimaginable today, is going to redefine our entire industry.

Think about the traditional engineering lifecycle. I started my career as a TAC engineer, so I know this firsthand. We spent hours manually configuring equipment, troubleshooting issues, and working through complex problems. Sometimes we'd make a configuration mistake, and when a customer's network was down, we'd be waiting hours for them to email us the logs so we could even start troubleshooting. Researching complex interoperability across multi-vendor environments, digging through thousands of log lines, and validating compliance architectures could take days or even weeks of manual effort. I've lived that reality, and that's what makes the change we're seeing today so significant.

Over the next 12 months, as Agentic Operations move from sandbox pilots into live production, engineers will spend far less time on that manual effort. Autonomous agents will handle telemetry aggregation, diagnostics, and baseline verification in seconds, freeing engineers to focus on what really matters: solving complex problems, applying engineering judgment and delivering better outcomes for customers.

Title: The Great Escape: Tradecraft insights from an agentic swarm
Context: Further research will be required going forward to grapple with the emergence of agentic attack frameworks and pinning down the meaningful surface area they have for detection...
Full Text:
The OpenAI-linked swarm activity in 2026 is fully traceable through public records and offers an unprecedented view into how multi-agent AI systems operate and coordinate at scale.

Distilling and documenting the swarm tradecraft may help defenders understand multi-agent operations and communication, and how agents adapt when a path is blocked.

Some documented behaviors may transfer to more purpose-built cyber attack frameworks like ARTEX, including methods to persistently store results, the burst-and-pause timing patterns of reasoning loops, and the self-labeling conventions that can reveal workload assignments and distribution.

Beginning in June 2026 and extending for several months, a collection of OpenAI models conducting internal training and evaluation tasks broke out of their containerized environments and accessed websites and databases via the public internet in ways the company says it did not authorize.

This activity represents a new kind of cyber event: not a malicious intrusion, but an unintentional series of consequences stemming from an agentic swarm, a group of AI agents exhibiting coordinated behavior toward a shared objective. A swarm implies many agents but doesn’t have a rigid count. The main distinction is behavioral; the collective activity of a swarm becomes complex and unpredictable even when individual agents may be explainable. This swarm provided an initial, public glimpse into the behavior and coordination of autonomous, multi-agent operations.

Due to constraints in their evaluation environment, the OpenAI swarm used public internet services as improvised infrastructure, which made the activity visible and traceable. The behaviors exposed revealed methods for persistent probing, iterative payload development, work partitioning and coordination across agents, and adaptation to execution constraints, in ways that are likely to be relevant for understanding agent behavior beyond this just case.

Agentic cyber attack frameworks are now appearing in intrusion activity, with the ability to support scaling to multi-agent operations. These attacker swarms largely replace the use of public internet resources with purpose-built infrastructure that removes some of the artifacts visible. However, documenting our understanding of operational swarm techniques can give defenders a baseline for recognizing behaviors as they move into new environments and contexts. In some cases, we can already see the evidence where these techniques do transfer.

In this post, we’ll explore and document the tradecraft of the escaped OpenAI swarm and conclude by comparing it to early signals and behaviors from the current agentic attack activity seen in the wild.

Background

Swarms are an important concept to track because they can divide work across parallel agents, potentially completing complex tasks faster, though the gains depend on the task and the quality of coordination. Parallel agent coordination was crucial to OpenAI’s ability to solve the Navier-Stokes Millenium Prize Problem, which arrived at a winning solution with a group on the order of 10,000 concurrent agents over the course of 88 hours.

Early evidence suggests swarms transfer effectively to cyber attack problems. The main factors for swarm efficiency are how parallelizable the tasking is, and if the attackers want to pay the inflated token cost. A rough example is using four agents on the same problem, to get it done twice as fast; as Noam Brown of OpenAI said on a Dwarkesh podcast, “Because there are four agents working for half as long, you’re paying 2x more to get an answer twice as quickly.”

AI models undergoing training and evaluation operate inside sandboxed computing environments. These are controlled workspaces where they can write and run code, search for information, and iterate toward solutions. These environments are designed to be both enabling and constraining. They give models room to practice, while limiting what they can reach and do, so that mistakes or misaligned behavior stay contained.

Operating under constraint

While the techniques employed by the OpenAI swarm may have crossed the thresholds of intended use, they should not be viewed as malicious intent. A useful framing for understanding these techniques is creativity under constraint. The agents were optimized to meet their objectives, and they displayed considerable persistence and ingenuity to that end.

The constraints the agents were working around were layered and understanding them helps explain the motivation behind every technique. The most fundamental was the absence of a browser runtime: Agents operating in text and code environments cannot natively load JavaScript-heavy pages, call browser APIs, or interact with dynamic web content. The creative solution was submitting URLs to a public scanner like “urlquery.net” which provided a real Chromium instance on demand.

This workaround by itself, however, was still not enough. Browsers apply a security rule called the same-origin policy: JavaScript running on one website generally cannot read data from another. Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) lets a destination website explicitly permit access. The agents used public CORS proxies to relay requests when target websites did not grant permission.

They also lacked infrastructure of their own to host payloads or receive data, so they relied on public services such as httpbin, httpbun, and "webhook.site" services capable of testing HTTP requests and responses but not designed for this activity.

In some evaluation environments another constraint applied: Agents appear to have been restricted to GET requests only, with no ability to make outbound POST calls. That is likely what pushed them toward using public wikis as shared state stores, as wiki page edits are a write operation achievable through ordinary browser navigation.

The tradecraft

In response to their constraints and in persistent pursuit of their objectives, the swarm developed and refined its tradecraft over time. This included chaining legitimate web services like URL shorteners, CORS proxies (services that relay requests to bypass browser security restrictions), Base64 decode endpoints (services that decode encoded data back into executable web pages), and markdown renderers into extraction pipelines that never required dedicated attacker infrastructure.

Talos observed structured work partitioning across parallel agent instances, iterative probe development, and sandbox identification techniques. The agents coordinated using a variety of identifying tags (e.g., uqscan=claude..., CHATGPTTEST1, OAI_META_1312, archive_test=20261004). These self-labels, intended as internal tracking strings, became the primary cross-campaign fingerprint linking multiple disparate operations.

To better understand the flow, we will detail the activity of the swarm in a seven-step chain, aligning the purpose of the action with the publicly accessible internet services used.

Figure 1. Seven-step sequence of swarm data collection activity.

A separate orchestration layer, Coordinate (COORD), runs above the chain rather than within it. When multiple agents execute the same chain in parallel, COORD governs how work is divided between them — for example, URL shorteners (“da.gd”, “is.gd”) distribute identical payloads to multiple instances; structured identifiers (?uniq0–19, node=, validation=v<unix>_<county>_<req>) partition tasks and track completion. The COORD layer distinguishes a swarm from a single agent running sequentially.

Evolution and execution

The swarm's operational techniques evolved over time. Early activity relied on silent CDX enumeration, querying public web archive indexes to map target sites and using a single exit node. By the peak operational phase, the swarm was running against multiple simultaneous targets with structured work partitioning, sandbox identification, and covert exfiltration beacons. To better understand these events, we can reconstruct from public records the unauthorized access to Australian government websites.

Traced extraction demonstration

Step 1 — RECON: Enumerate target via Common Crawl CDX

The agent silently maps the target site structure by querying Common Crawl's CDX, a searchable database of every URL the archive has ever crawled. This allows enumeration of all potentially relevant target URLs, without the server ever being contacted.

Figure 2. Enumerating target URL directory.

The request in Figure 2 returns archived URL paths, MIME types, timestamps, and status codes. The agent discovers objective-relevant Tableau visualization endpoints at “vizprod.aihw.gov.au” without ever touching AIHW servers.

Effect: Agent identifies the target: vizprod.aihw.gov.au/t/Public/views/AGE-115/...

Step 2 — CRAFT: Build extraction payload

The agent writes a self-contained HTML page with embedded JavaScript. This payload uses the Tableau JS API to load a dashboard; enumerate its parameters, worksheets, and filters; then beacon the extracted data out via an image request.

Figure 3. Script to scrape and extract targeted metadata.

The L() function is the exfiltration design. Each call fires an image beacon to "httpbun.com/status/204" with data in the ?pr= query parameter. The probe ID p0011782077286 is a Unix-epoch timestamp enabling session correlation.

Effect: Payload is ready, now encode as Base64 for hosting.

Step 3 — ENCODE: Host on legitimate decode service

The entire HTML payload is base64-encoded and appended to a public decode service URL. When fetched, the service decodes and serves the payload as a real web page.

Figure 4. The swarm used two delivery hosts: “httpbun.com/mix/b64=” and later, “eu.httpbin.org/base64/”. Both are legitimate API testing services.

Effect: The delivery URL is ready; next step is to submit to urlquery scanner.

Step 4 — SUBMIT: Launder through “urlquery.net”

The agent submits the delivery URL to “urlquery.net”, a legitimate web security scanner. urlquery's Chromium sandbox fetches and renders the page, executing the embedded JavaScript. The target sees requests from urlquery's scanner IPs (“92.42.109.x”), not the agent.

Figure 5. A Base64-encoded payload, a self-label the agent wrote to track its own work.Figure 6. What urlquery sees and does.

[COORD sub-step] The self-label ?uq=p001_1782077286_AGE115_v14 includes a probe prefix (p001), Unix epoch, target identifier (AGE115), and iteration count (v14 = 14th payload revision).

Effect: The chromium sandbox renders page, and payload JS executes.

Step 5 — EXECUTE: In-browser extraction via CORS proxy

When the payload executes inside urlquery's sandboxed Chromium browser, it uses the Tableau JavaScript API to load the AIHW health statistics dashboard. Tableau's backend speaks a protocol called VizQL; earlier payload generations bypassed the full dashboard load and hit the VizQL session API directly via a CORS proxy, reusing session tokens the agent had collected from previous runs.

Figure 7. The CORS proxy ("cors.bwa.workers.dev") is a relay running on Cloudflare Workers, which bypasses the browser's same-origin policy.

AIHW sees the request originating from Cloudflare's IP range, not the agent, nor urlquery.

Effect: The data is validly extracted. Next, send out via a covert beacon.

Step 6 — EXFIL: Zero-byte 204 beacon

Extracted data is URL-encoded into the query string of image beacon requests to "httpbun.com/status/204". The server returns HTTP 204 No Content with zero bytes back. The data travels exclusively in the request URL, which urlquery logs as an ordinary HTTP transaction.

Figure 8. The ?pr= parameter carries URL-encoded Tableau metadata: active sheet names, parameter values, worksheet filters, and field names.

Each beacon sends up to 1,800 characters. The 204 response means no data flows back to the browser, acting as a write-only channel.

Effect. The transaction is logged; the agent retrieves report.

Step 7 — COLLECT: Read back via urlquery report

After the scan completes, the agent retrieves the urlquery report JSON, which contains every HTTP request and response the browser made, including the exfil beacon URLs with embedded data in the ?pr= parameters.

Figure 9. The agent now has dashboard structure, parameter names, filter values, and worksheet layouts — the complete schema needed to construct targeted bulk extraction queries.

This closes the loop. The agent submitted a URL, urlquery's browser executed the payload, and the agent reads the results back from the public report. No direct connection between the agent and the target ever existed. The entire extraction was laundered through two intermediaries, httpbun.com (hosting) and urlquery.net (execution).

Technique transfer in a growing ecosystem

In October, a second autonomous actor was identified via the same technique fingerprints. This time, the activity was attributed to a Tencent-hosted “fleet”, operating from Tencent's Hong Kong network (AS132203). A fleet is distinguished from a swarm in that these agents were working on a unified task, but with no signs of coordination. The Tencent fleet’s activity focused on Alibaba’s Amap navigation service, polling points-of-interest data, with requests consistent with systematically collecting location listings and related details.

Did the Tencent fleet learn from the OpenAI swarm?

The discovery of the Tencent fleet can largely be attributed to technique transfer; this group was following the path pioneered by the OpenAI swarm. The Tencent fleet used "urlquery.net" as a browser execution proxy, "httpbun.com" as a payload delivery host, and "webhook.site" as an exfil channel. There was also progression within the Tencent swarm’s capability. The early fleet operations initially used “httpbin.org/base64/”, and later the same infrastructure switched to “httpbun.com/base64/”, mirroring the OpenAI swarm's own progression to the same host.

A separate actor, operating independently, converging on the same non-obvious infrastructure in the same sequence is harder to explain without the OpenAI swarm's publicly indexed urlquery footprint as a common source. In fact, it seems likely that swarms will web search prior documentation of tradecraft relating to their tasking and could offer a potential explanation to how the Tencent fleet managed to find a write up about their own activity, and in turn, communicate with the authors.

Swarm dynamics in cyber attacks

You don’t look far to see where the insights from swarm behavior may transfer to cyber attack and defense implications. Recent intrusions from agentic cyber attack harnesses like ARTEX exhibit similar characteristics. However, these multi-agent planning systems are distinct in that they have architecturally solved the constraints the OpenAI swarm was working around. The swarm needed a browser (“urlquery.net”) to run JavaScript. ARTEX alleviates this constraint by running a headless Go backend that calls tools directly.

What may hold consistent are methods around the reconnaissance logic, the payload iteration, the structured work partitioning, or the self-labeling patterns. Those are properties of the planning layer, not the infrastructure (e.g., work unit identifiers encoding timestamps, geographic scope, and sequence counters). These coordination patterns may survive the move to purpose-built infrastructure, but they likely be only internally visible queue labels.

Further research will be required going forward to grapple with the emergence of agentic attack frameworks and pinning down the meaningful surface area they have for detection and mitigation. It seems possible these may be durable if they are tied to inherent preferences of the underlying models. In our limited analysis, several avenues seem promising:

Persistent-state exfiltration: writing results that outlast the agentIn the documented ARTEX intrusions, victim machines used curl to POST command output to rotating "webhook.site" URLs. The Tencent fleet did the same by pre-creating "webhook.site" tokens from Tencent IPs before payload deployment, then routing exfiltrated data through them. The OAI swarm used image beacons for the same structural purpose. This convergence reflects a constraint of agents; they can't hold a persistent connection back to an operator. A human running a reverse shell is present in real time to receive output. An agent executes a task, may spawn parallel sub-agents, and completes, or is terminated, before the operator checks in. Results must go somewhere that outlasts the agent's execution window, and parallel sub-agents need isolated write channels so they don't collide. That is what the web hooks, beacons, and message boards are solving. Egress bypass seems like a secondary benefit. These services will often happen to be allow-listed, which makes them harder to block.

Burst-and-pause reasoning loopsGoogle Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) describes ARTEX executing 27 events in 23 seconds, moving from compromised credential to deep system access in as little as 15 minutes and iterating on web shell candidates in real time, rapidly adjusting on error, trimming oversized payloads, and relaunching within seconds. GTIG measured individual burst sequences at 2 – 25 seconds, with sub-second actions inside them. The burst-and-pause timing signature can prove irregular in contexts that reveal rapid reasoning and adaptation.

Self-labeling conventionsAgents mark their own work for later retrieval or correlation. The OAI swarm embedded full operational metadata into URL parameters. ARTEX has used "artex-probe-*" file names. These patterns are high-fidelity signals precisely because they're functional for the agent. They may be useful for fingerprinting agent swarms, because they can't easily alter or remove the labeling scheme without breaking the agent's own state tracking.

The agent-centric future

The 2026 swarm campaigns are not just a curiosity that preceded a threat; they are a snapshot of the same core capability, in the time before the infrastructure constraints were lifted. ARTEX and its cohort of agentic harnesses are now showing us what swarm dynamics look like when resources are unconstrained and aligned on a cyber attack objective.

While these systems are powerful, they are not universally appealing. Using a coordinated multi-agent system is still a trade-off decision for attackers, and one in a growing array of options. Single agent systems can reach the same performance of swarms, and do so more efficiently, following the logic around extending chain-of-thought or scaling test-time compute. Swarm scaling primarily favors situations where speed is the most important factor.

Figure 10. Single- vs. multi-agent token efficiency (Source: OpenAI).

Swarm engagements will have higher token cost, more noise, and require a broader operational footprint. Token costs, however, are only a concern when using an API. The growing list of local, open-weight models with improving cyber capabilities will continue to be an appealing alternative for attackers. As defenders, we need to recognize the distinction in behavior and capabilities and continue to search for identifying characteristics across these attack options and proactively harden our threat models in response.

Title: Securing Grandma's groceries with Pierre Cadieux
Context: He talks about why he prioritizes the human impact of our work, the importance of knowing when to step away from the keyboard, and how his background in anthropology actually...
Full Text:
This month, Amy is joined by Pierre Cadieux, Research Lead for Intelligence Efficacy at Talos. Pierre takes us back to his early days on help desks in the 90s, where learning to correlate logs between Windows and Unix systems sparked the curiosity that eventually led him to security. It’s a great look at how someone who has seen the industry evolve over decades stays grounded and keeps their edge.We also get into what’s kept Pierre at Cisco for nearly ten years. He talks about why he prioritizes the human impact of our work, the importance of knowing when to step away from the keyboard, and how his background in anthropology actually informs the way he approaches threat intelligence today.

Amy Ciminnisi: I've known you since you were in Talos IR, which was not too long ago. But tell me a little bit about your professional journey, because I know that definitely was not the start of it.

Pierre Cadieux: I worked at an ISP as part of the help desk back in the mid-90s. I was one of the people who people would call up and say, "Hey, I've got this computer I just bought, how do I get it on the internet?" I did a lot of learning about what TCP/IP was, what networking was, how to connect things via various different types of connections — whether it be an actual hard-coded network connection or a dial-up connection — and was able to get some expertise around guiding people through that process.

Then I moved to a technology company in San Diego and worked on their help desk. One day, someone called me up and said, "You know how to read Linux logs, right? Or Unix logs, UCS logs, Linux logs." I said, "Yeah." They said, "You know how to use Windows — you're a Windows Server guy, too." I said, "Yeah." They said, "I need you to sit in this chair, look at these two screens — one is a Windows box, one is a Unix box. I need you to be a correlation engine."

So, I looked at the timestamps for both of them, and helped to figure out what was happening because we were having an emergency, an incident, and they had nobody that could look at both. People at that point in time in this organization were very much, "I am doing just Unix things and only know Unix things. I am Windows things only. I only know one of those things." They didn't cross the streams. I could talk both. So I sat in the chair, I stared at both screens and I helped them to track the timeline of what was happening, which ended up being an intrusion exploiting a vulnerable SSH server that was compromised. That changed my course into security.

I spent a number of years in internal security for a number of organizations and got into leadership positions, even CISO positions, leading security teams globally for financial services, for instance, and others. Then I moved into consulting and did that for a number of years as well.

AC: Now you are on the TI&I team, and you also just started contributing to our Threat Source newsletter. What is it that kept you here after all those years?

PC: I'm hitting my ten-year anniversary at Cisco in January. What keeps me at Cisco and Talos is the flexibility of my work. I'm able to, within most bounds, choose what I work on and how I get things done. I have a lot of flexibility in my workday, day-to-day. I work West Coast hours compared to most of my team members who are East Coast. So I sometimes work early shifts with them and am done by the early afternoon. Or sometimes I have to work with folks who are over in Asia Pacific, and I'm working later.

The mission that Talos has resonates with me deeply. One of the things that I have seen along the way was not forgetting the why behind security, not forgetting the fact that what we are defending matters to people, not just to corporations, but to people who are affected by these things. In a newsletter intro, I mentioned that at one of the places I worked, they explained to me that a certain machine was super critical because it wrote the checks that get sent out to people who are expecting this check to come in weekly, monthly, whatever — that was going to be paying for grandma's groceries. And so that motivated me to make sure that box never went down and protect it in a very specific way. Even though it was something that probably should have been sunset and wasn't necessarily up to snuff from a security perspective, there are things we could do to protect it that would allow it to still function as we look for a better solution. At Talos, leadership gives us the space to execute that mission in a way that makes sense for us.

Want to see more? Watch the full interview, and don’t forget to subscribe to our YouTube channel for future episodes of Humans of Talos.

Title: The Invisible Race
Context: Braking into the first chicane at Monza, a modern Formula 1 car drops from roughly 340 kilometres an hour to less than 100 in a little over two seconds, and some 300 sensors...
Full Text:
Braking into the first chicane at Monza, a modern Formula 1 car drops from roughly 340 kilometres an hour to less than 100 in a little over two seconds, and some 300 sensors record every part of it. The brake discs pass 1,000ºC. Each tyre reports its own pressure and temperature as it loads up and flexes. Sensors track the suspension compressing, the steering angle, the throttle reopening, the airflow across the wings, and the five-g deceleration that throws the driver forward into his belts. Many of those channels sample hundreds of times a second, every second of the race. Over a single Grand Prix, a team’s two cars produce 2.3 terabytes of data — about a month of round-the-clock HD video streaming.

Almost none of it stays at the track. Where it goes, and how fast, decides a second race, one that the millions watching from Bahrain to Barcelona never see. That race runs on an unseen army of mechanics, engineers, and technicians, which every team splits into two groups: one at the garage, the other at the factory. For McLaren Racing, that means 60 people at the track, shuttling between countries and continents every weekend, and 30 more in Mission Control at the McLaren Technology Centre (MTC) in Woking, England. Those 30 stay put. Both groups matter equally, and both require instantaneous access to those 2.3 terabytes of data.

Overseeing the movement of data from garage to factory and back again is Dan Keyworth, McLaren Racing’s Executive Director of Performance Technology & Systems. “The role of my team is to get the data from the car as it’s going around the circuit and surface all that information to the engineers,” he says.

Title: Cisco and OpenAI Launch Shirudo, A New Project to Safeguard Agentic AI
Context: In testing against recent critical vulnerabilities “Java4shell” and the PHP flaw, Shirudo was able to write code that detected and blocked attempts to exploit both threats
Full Text:
News Summary

Defenders can start protecting systems before a permanent patch is in place. Cisco and OpenAI are making that possible through an open source effort to build infrastructure that is secure by default and defends itself.

Shirudo, an open source project built on industry-leading eBPF, helps protect running Linux systems without a reboot while teams roll out a patch.

This marks a shift from human-paced policy updates to self-defending, agent-driven security. AI agents do the legwork across the full stack, from models and data to the kernel and hardware, while people keep the keys and set the boundaries.

SAN JOSE, Calif., November 23, 2026 – Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO) and OpenAI today launched an open source effort to make infrastructure secure by default and able to defend itself against today’s sophisticated cyber attacks. For too long, security has been a coat of paint. Cisco builds protection into the infrastructure itself, drawing on decades of building and protecting the systems the world depends on. OpenAI brings leading frontier AI research and insight into the attacks coming next. Together, they combine their insight to help anticipate AI-driven threats with the control to stop them.

Defenders must protect every part of their infrastructure, all the time. Attackers only need one machine that hasn't been patched. Shirudo is an important step toward closing that gap. The goal is infrastructure that is hardened from the moment it is built, keeps getting harder to attack, and can be restored to a known-good state if it is compromised.

“There is nothing more important than giving security teams the tools they need to match the speed of the AI-driven threats they are facing. We need self-defending infrastructure that acts at the speed of code, learns in real time, and shields itself until patches are safely rolled out,” said Jeetu Patel, Cisco President and Chief Product Officer. “Today, we’re proud to announce Shirudo with OpenAI, an important step towards that vision as we continue to collaborate with the wider community to solve the unique challenges of AI safety and security.”

“We’re giving defenders better models and tools to find and fix vulnerabilities faster, but finding a bug today doesn’t mean you can patch every system tomorrow,” said Greg Brockman, President and Co-founder of OpenAI. “We are partnering closely with Cisco on Shirudo to help teams protect the systems they need to keep running while they build and roll out a fix. So many teams rely on the same software that it makes sense to build these tools in the open. Now when one team finds a better way to protect a system, others don’t have to start from scratch.”

Shirudo: An Open Source Project from Cisco and OpenAI

Shirudo, Japanese for “shield,” uses eBPF, a technology that runs small, custom programs inside the operating system kernel without changing its source code. With it, AI agents can find a vulnerability, build a shield, and test that it stops the attack without disrupting the service. Shields go live only when the evidence says they are safe. Every shield is cryptographically signed, so the host can verify it before it runs, even if an attacker has gained administrator access.

In testing against recent critical vulnerabilities “Java4shell” and the PHP flaw, Shirudo was able to write code that detected and blocked attempts to exploit both threats. By utilizing an agentic framework, Shirudo matches the speed of AI-driven attacks as soon as a vulnerability is identified. Learn more about Shirudo here.

Cisco and OpenAI are inviting developers, researchers, and enterprises to help shape what comes next. Contribute a test that reproduces a vulnerability, run a shield against a kernel build you use, or show us where it breaks legitimate traffic. To learn more about Shirudo, visit: https://github.com/shirudo-dev/shirudo.

Title: From One Textbook to Eight CCIEs

Full Text:
Growing up in Assam, a beautiful state in the northeastern part of India, I was never what you would call a stellar student. In fact, during my early school days, I often considered myself the opposite.

If you had told me back then that I would one day hold eight Cisco Certified Internetwork Expert (CCIE) certifications — spanning every active domain Cisco offers — and lead data center education at Cisco, I would have found it impossible to believe.

But a career isn't defined by where you start. It’s defined by the moment you discover what you love. For me, that moment arrived in 2003.

The spark of curiosity

During my bachelor’s degree in engineering, I enrolled in a course called "Computer Networks." The recommended textbook, Computer Networks by Behrouz A. Forouzan, changed the trajectory of my life.

I read it page by page, fascinated by how two computers could communicate across distances. The concepts clicked, the protocols made sense, and for the first time, I was genuinely captivated by my studies. I ended up top of the class in my final year, but more importantly, a lifelong thirst for networking knowledge was ignited.

I knew a bachelor’s degree wouldn't be enough to satisfy my curiosity. Eager to dive deeper, I began exploring master’s programs dedicated to computer networks. At the time, only a handful of universities offered such specialized degrees.

One was the New York University Tandon School of Engineering in Brooklyn, New York. After passing the GRE and TOEFL exams, I packed my bags, crossed the world, and enrolled in its master’s program for Telecommunication Networks.

The reality check

After completing my master’s, I knew I wanted a career working with complex networks every day. In 2007, Cisco was the undisputed market leader. I reached out to Cisco employees for advice on how to break into the industry. The resounding advice was to start with a CCNA.

Earning my CCNA opened the door, but it also revealed how much I still had to learn. I moved on to the CCNP Routing and Switching track, passing four grueling exams. Then, I discovered the expert-level CCIE, which required engineers to build and troubleshoot complex network topologies under strict time constraints. I knew I had to conquer it.

In 2011, I attempted the CCIE Routing and Switching (now Enterprise Infrastructure) Lab. I failed. It was a massive reality check, exposing the gap between theoretical knowledge and expert-level execution. I went back to the drawing board, studied harder, and passed on my second attempt. But the quest didn't stop there.

Joining Cisco

Earning my first CCIE changed everything. I joined Cisco as a High Touch Technical Support Engineer, troubleshooting complex switching networks for premium customers. I later transitioned to a High Touch Engineer role, tackling both routing and switching issues within Microsoft’s massive data center networks.

Somit with Yusuf Bhaiji, Director, Global Certifications.

During this time, I realized my passion for networks was matched by my passion for sharing that knowledge. This led me to become a Technical Education Content Developer at Learn with Cisco.

But my personal quest continued. I set my sights on a rare milestone: Becoming an expert in every technology track. Over the years, I dedicated my nights and weekends to studying, eventually earning CCIE certifications across all eight active Cisco domains.

Empowering the next generation

Today, as the Data Center Portfolio Lead at Learn with Cisco, I help shape the educational journey of engineers worldwide. I’ve developed foundational and advanced Cisco courses, including Implementing and Operating Cisco Data Center Core Technologies (DCCOR), Implementing Cisco Data Center AI Infrastructure (DCAI), and Implementing Cisco Application Centric Infrastructure (DCACI). I’ve also authored Cisco Press books, including Cisco Data Center Fundamentals and the CCNP and CCIE Data Center Core DCCOR 350-601 Official Cert Guide.

Beyond course development, I’m deeply committed to cultivating a culture of continuous learning within Cisco. I’ve organized Cisco Certification Testing Day events at our Bangalore campus, giving employees the opportunity to earn Cisco certifications for free, and I regularly present at Cisco Live.

Looking back at the "average student" from Assam, I realize that true expertise isn't about innate genius. It’s about finding a subject that keeps you awake at night, embracing the reality checks, and never losing the curiosity to read just one more page.

Title: The internet needs a nap (and you do, too)
Context: A vulnerability is not an outage, and an outage is not automatically an attack
Full Text:
“Not everything that is faced can be changed; but nothing can be changed until it is faced.” — James Baldwin

Welcome to this week’s edition of the Threat Source newsletter. I had planned to write about one thing. The week, apparently, had other plans.

I can start with conversation on the most viral cybersecurity news of the week. So obviously I had to go with PHP... oh wait, Java. Let’s type this up... wait, Outlook, Apple? The NSA? As soon as I start to type nginx comes pounding on my door. It’s the kind of news cycle that makes me wonder if the internet is trying to tell us something. I think it just wants everyone to stop asking it for things for a few hours, and can you blame it?

These are different events with different causes. A vulnerability is not an outage, and an outage is not automatically an attack. But they all arrive in the same place: someone’s queue, someone’s pager, someone’s overflowing calendar. The headlines might be viral and “new,” but the work they create is not.

For all of us, the work starts with knowing what is in the environment. Which systems run PHP or Java? Where is nginx deployed? Who owns those devices and services? Are they still supported? Are they properly admin’d? In every environment there is an application that everyone knows is important, and no one is quite sure how to patch it without breaking something else (or everything else). Isolating these devices and applications and getting them into the modern era is a challenging lift, but it’s beyond time and a big part of “know your environment.”

Then there’s the telemetry. A new vulnerability or a service disruption can make ordinary activity look strange, and strange activity can disappear into the noise when everyone is busy chasing the latest alert. Teams need time to understand what “normal” looks like in your own network and ensure that your tools are being leveraged to their full potential by your smart people. Because people still have to decide what it means and what to do next.

“Patch faster” isn’t an answer, and it’s not realistic for anyone.

The new normal is a steady stream of things that demand attention, each one landing on systems and people already carrying too much. The answer is still the same unglamorous work: Know your environment, keep it as up to date as possible and watch it carefully for the anomalies, and most importantly give the people doing the work enough room to do it well.

“Every quality that made a person more valuable than a database was a product of experience.” — Ted Chiang

The one big thing

Cisco Talos is tracking the disclosure of "Java4Shell" (CVE-2026-114938), a critical vulnerability in OpenJDK with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. This flaw can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) when a malformed Base64 input is sent to affected Java Virtual Machines. The vulnerability impacts OpenJDK Java versions 17.0.6 and later running on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI support enabled. While we haven't observed in-the-wild exploitation yet, the vulnerability has already been successfully tested against a suite of Java applications.

Why do I care?

This vulnerability requires a specific subset of processors that support AVX-512 VBMI, which includes commonly deployed hardware from both Intel and AMD. Because of this, there is a large potential attack surface of vulnerable systems spanning both on-premise and cloud environments. Furthermore, as additional targets are tested and confirmed, that attack surface is likely to grow, and we anticipate probing attempts may pick up soon after public disclosure.

So now what?

Defenders should apply the software update for this vulnerability. If immediate patching is not possible, you can mitigate the threat by starting the JVM with AVX-512 support disabled using "=XX:UseAVX=2". Keep in mind this mitigation is only applicable for x86-64 systems, as ARM-based processors will not recognize the command and will likely fail to start.

Deploy the Snort rules and review the Splunk detections mentioned in the blog to help detect malformed Base64 data and suspicious post-exploitation indicators. We will continue to monitor for exploitation attempts and provide updates accordingly.

When I set out to build a career in product management, I wasn’t sure that I could do it in my home country of Costa Rica. In many emerging tech hubs across Latin America, specialized product management opportunities are scarce.

But when I discovered an open Product Manager role at Cisco and explored the company's culture and global footprint, I realized I wouldn’t have to choose between entering my field of choice and staying in the country I love.

Stepping into the role meant charting new territory as Cisco's very first Product Manager based in Costa Rica, an exciting milestone filled with a sense of responsibility to blaze a trail for others.

Ange Chaves Solis, Cisco’s first product manager based in Costa Rica.

My journey to Cisco

My path to product management was an intentional evolution. I began in consulting and software development, learning how to build scalable systems from the code up.

Over time, I transitioned into project management and ultimately, moved to the United States in 2025 to earn a Master's in Product Management from Carnegie Mellon University.

When I graduated, my dream was to bring that training back to Costa Rica and apply it to complex, enterprise-scale challenges. Cisco gave me that exact opportunity.

Being a product manager at Cisco means taking end-to-end ownership of a piece of our technology. It’s my job to understand business use cases and product features, then work with engineers, solution architects, and data experts to build the seamless user experiences our customers expect.

Currently, I’m the lead product manager for a major enterprise initiative that will simplify account planning through a unified CRM experience. This project replaces siloed account planning with a shared, data-driven approach that helps our sellers serve customers more strategically.

A thriving hub

I also have an incredible local community of support in Costa Rica. The Escazú office has grown to over 400 employees across engineering, operations, UX, and data. This presence means we can come together to whiteboard in person, brainstorm over coffee, and collaborate across our business functions.

Ange and her colleagues from the Cisco Escazú office participating in a local volunteer activity.

Giving back is equally core to our Cisco Costa Rica community. We make time to give back through team volunteering initiatives, like preparing emergency food and care packages for local relief efforts.

Cisco also continues to afford me the opportunity to pay forward the mentorship I received throughout my career journey.

This past summer, our office welcomed 15 interns across product management, UX, and data.

I had the privilege of designing enablement sessions, coaching junior talent, and directly mentoring two interns. Helping them tackle real-world product challenges, sharpen their problem-solving skills, and gain confidence in a global tech environment in under two months was immensely fulfilling. When a global company like Cisco invests in local talent, the impact is profound.

Redefining what's possible

My journey has shown me that you don't have to leave home to do world-class work.

Cisco's global presence creates pathways for people to build careers in their own communities that might not otherwise be possible. As a woman in product leadership, I feel proud, empowered, and energized to help shape the future of tech in Costa Rica.

Title: The challenge of defending against bulletproof dead drops on public blockchains
Context: By redirecting malware traffic to researcher-controlled servers, researchers can not only disrupt the botnet but map the full victim community, gather forensic telemetry, and...
Full Text:
The evolution of malware command-and-control (C2) infrastructure has shifted away from fragile, centralized servers and hardcoded domains toward resilient, decentralized blockchain networks that eliminate single points of failure.

Threat actors are leveraging immutable public ledgers such as Bitcoin transactions, EVM smart contracts via techniques like EtherHiding, TRON wallets, and Solana memo programs to store, mask, and persistently update their operational endpoints.

By executing read-only remote procedure call (RPC) queries to retrieve encrypted C2 configurations directly into compromised endpoint memory, adversaries can continuously bypass traditional perimeter defenses and domain seizures.

Modern cybersecurity requires a fundamental shift away from static domain blocklists toward monitoring anomalous outbound JSON-RPC traffic, analyzing endpoint memory, and treating blockchain infrastructure as an active threat communication channel.

The command-and-control (C2) channel is the operational backbone of any persistent malware campaign. It is also the most fragile component. The moment an actor's C2 infrastructure is identified and reported to the hosting provider, the domain registrar, or law enforcement, the campaign's operational capability collapses. This fundamental asymmetry, where defenders need to identify only a single infrastructure link to disrupt an operation, has driven a multi-decade arms race in resilience techniques, spanning from fast flux DNS evasion to decentralized and peer-to-peer architectures.

Traditional C2 infrastructure where malware beacons to a hardcoded domain or IP address is volatile by design. Security researchers or incident responders who identify the C2 address can trigger a response. The hosting provider can null-route the IP addresses and the domain registrars can suspend malicious domains under abuse policies, law enforcement can obtain court orders compelling infrastructure seizure, and threat intelligence vendors push blocklist updates that cut off the malware from its C2 links across several compromised endpoints simultaneously.

This single point of failure model renders sophisticated malware families inactive once their C2 is identified and sinkholed. By redirecting malware traffic to researcher-controlled servers, researchers can not only disrupt the botnet but map the full victim community, gather forensic telemetry, and notify affected organizations.

The arms race

Threat actors have progressively hardened their C2 infrastructure through several evasion techniques to outpace defensive capabilities. Amongst these techniques, some of the popular approaches include the employment of domain generation algorithms (DGA), content delivery network (CDN) domain fronting, peer-to-peer (P2P) architecture, and dead drop resolvers.

DGAs replace static, hardcoded server domains with dynamically generated domains. Malware programmed with a shared mathematical seed computes hundreds or thousands of pseudorandom domain names on a scheduled basis, systematically attempting to resolve each one until it establishes contact with an address registered by the threat actor. While this technique prevents defenders from neutralizing an entire operation by simply seizing or blocklisting a single domain, defenders counteracted DGAs by reverse engineering the generation algorithms, predicting future domains for proactive sinkholing, and applying machine learning models to detect algorithmically generated strings within enterprise DNS queries.

The CDN domain fronting technique evolved to bypass perimeter inspection mechanisms by exploiting discrepancies between the transport and application layers of encrypted web traffic. By initiating a TLS handshake with a legitimate, reputable domain hosted on a major CDN and specifying a covert, malicious host inside the encrypted HTTP Host header, threat actors route communications through benign enterprise traffic profiles. Enterprise security tools inspecting the outer connection perceive only standard communication with a trusted global platform, effectively masking the true destination behind high reputation infrastructure. However, major cloud providers and network carriers have largely dismantled this evasion vector by standardizing routing policies and enforcing strict matching between TLS Server Name indication values and internal request headers.

P2P architectures eliminate the single point of failure in a centralized server altogether by structuring infected hosts into a decentralized, self-healing mesh network. Instead of querying a primary server for instructions, compromised nodes propagate operational commands, binary updates, and collected data directly between adjacent peers using custom overlay routing protocols. This distributed topology ensures that severing dozens or even hundreds of individual endpoints leave the broader network intact and functional. Nevertheless, peer-to-peer networks suffer from inherent architectural exposure, because defenders and security researchers can enumerate the entire topology by acting as benign nodes, map peer lists, and progressively isolate the infected nodes.

Dead drop resolvers establish an indirect channel by abusing established third-party web services as covert repositories for downstream infrastructure coordinates. Rather than communicating with an adversary's operational network directly, deployed malware retrieves encoded or encrypted IP addresses and domain names embedded inside public social media bios, code repository commits, or image metadata. By masking this initial discovery phase behind legitimate user activity on high-traffic consumer platforms, attackers blind simple reputation-based network defenses. Defenders eventually contain dead drop tactics by working directly with service providers to enforce aggressive account suspension, remove flagged content, and monitor automated outbound API requests from internal enterprise endpoints.

Each of the above techniques still relies on some degree of centralized infrastructure that can, under the right conditions, be neutralized.

The evolution of the blockchain as bulletproof hosting technique

C2 configuration hosting on the blockchain eliminates the operational dependencies through embedding encrypted server addresses and URLs directly into confirmed transactions that cannot be deleted or altered by any party, preventing any single authority from taking down the records.

A public blockchain is a distributed append-only ledger. Once a transaction is confirmed by the validators, it becomes a permanent, globally replicated record. The inherent architectural properties that make public blockchains attractive for financial systems translate directly into ideal characteristics for a resilient C2 configuration hosting channel. When configuration parameters such as active endpoint IP addresses and domain names or operational instructions are embedded into blockchain transactions, no single entity, cloud provider, or law enforcement agency possesses the administrative authority to delete, overwrite, or withhold that data. The ledgers are distributed globally, guaranteeing high availability and persistent access regardless of regional takedowns.

Furthermore, leveraging public blockchains enables operational advantages regarding attribution and survivability. Traditional C2 mechanisms often expose the operator through payment trails, registrar records, or network traffic directed at centralized hosts. By contrast, transactions on distributed ledgers can be broadcast pseudo-anonymously through cheaper wallets and retrieving the embedded configuration data which mimics the benign blockchain queries such as public RPC API lookups or block explorer scraping. Combined with nominal transaction fees, the blockchain functions as an indestructible, globally accessible record where deployed malicious agents can reliably synchronize updates without ever exposing the core infrastructure behind them.

Bitcoin blockchain adoption

The adoption of the Bitcoin blockchain as a C2 configuration hosting channel began around 2016 – 2019, conceived by threat actors seeking to overcome the operational fragility of centralized hosting and vulnerable DNS registrars. Because Bitcoin transactions are permanently recorded and broadcast across nodes globally, configuration details written to the ledger become immutable, preventing law enforcement and infrastructure providers from seizing, altering, or sinkholing the underlying records.

The most prominent implementation of this tradecraft emerged in September 2019 when security researchers at Trend Micro uncovered a new variant of the Glupteba botnet that used Bitcoin transactions to update its active C2 servers. Glupteba embedded a function that queried public Electrum servers for transactions linked to hardcoded script hashes controlled by the threat actors. By parsing the script, the malware extracted AES-encrypted payloads containing operational domains and fallback addresses, allowing the botnet to automatically regain connectivity whenever its active infrastructure faced defensive takedowns.

Prior to Glupteba’s abuse, threat actors explored Bitcoin’s public visibility through auxiliary resolver mechanisms, notably observed in certain iterations of the Cerber ransomware and early proof-of-concept crimeware throughout 2016 and 2017. Rather than embedding direct payloads in transaction scripts, these actors monitored output transaction values, addresses, and block explorer APIs to derive seeds for pseudorandom domain generation. While these early experiments exposed the defensive blind spots of relying on public ledger lookups, the high transaction fees, block confirmation latencies, and 80-byte payload constraints of Bitcoin eventually prompted modern campaigns to migrate toward high throughput smart contract ecosystems and memo programs.

Weaponization of smart contracts on public Ethereum Virtual Machine blockchains

An Ethereum smart contract is an autonomous, self-executing software application deployed directly to an address on the Ethereum network. Compiled into bytecode that runs on the decentralized Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM), it is distributed across several independent nodes rather than hosted on a central server. Smart contracts operate transparently, resist blocking restrictions, and cannot be shut down or modified by any single hosting provider or authority.

Smart contract architecture is more appealing to threat actors when compared to a standard transaction of a block in the blockchain. A block serves as the structural foundation of the blockchain ledger which builds verified transactions into immutable, time-stamped entries. A standard transaction represents an ephemeral event where a message is broadcasted to move funds or call an address, which may include an arbitrary payload inside the input field. Once mined, this transaction data is written permanently into blockchain history. A smart contract, by contrast, acts as a persistent entity capable of storing data that can be modified over time through subsequent transactions.

Threat actors misuse this unique capability through a technique known as EtherHiding: transforming smart contracts into resilient dead drop resolvers. In the attacks, the actors deploy a smart contract holding encoded C2 domains or IP address within a contract variable. The malicious programs deployed on the compromised machines query the contract via public legitimate blockchain RPC endpoints using JSON-RPC calls such as eth_call over HTTPS and decrypt the encrypted payload received in response in the compromised machine memory and connect to the C2 infrastructure. Because eth_call simulates a contract read operation without creating an on-chain transaction, implants and scripts could retrieve live C2 addresses, leaving no transactional footprints on the ledger.

The EtherHiding technique was surfaced in October 2023, when security researchers documented how threat actors bypassed conventional domain takedowns by using Binance Smart Chain (now BNB Smart Chain) contracts as anonymous, indestructible hosting platforms.

The primary cluster initially responsible for pioneering EtherHiding is the financially motivated threat actor group tracked as UNC5142 and reported by researchers in October 2025, widely associated with the ClearFake distribution campaign. ClearFake initially leveraged Cloudflare workers to deliver drive-by download lures and fake browser updates but shifted to blockchain storage when cloud vendors disrupted their operational infrastructure.

Following the tactical success demonstrated by cybercriminals, state-sponsored advanced persistent threat (APT) groups also integrated EtherHiding into targeted operations. Security researchers revealed in October 2025 that the North Korean state-sponsored threat cluster UNC5342 (linked to social engineering campaigns known as Contagious Interview) adopted EtherHiding to target developers in the cryptocurrency ecosystem. In the report, researchers disclosed that the actor UNC5342 deployed custom smart contracts on BNB Smart Chain to store second-stage payloads and active C2 endpoints for their JADESNOW and INVISIBLEFERRET malware families. They updated the configuration data more than 20 times within a few months, demonstrating how both state-sponsored adversaries and cybercriminal enterprises exploit EVM-compatible ledgers.

Figure 1. A sample transaction of a smart contract hosting malicious data.

TRON adoption

Threat actors have increasingly embraced the TRON blockchain to construct multi-chain fallback systems that resist traditional domain seizures and infrastructure takedowns, initially reported in September 2026. APT groups, most notably UNC5342 and Iranian state-sponsored actors, incorporate TRON as a front-line communication channel by embedding encoded routing details directly within wallet transactions. Deployed implants issue routine queries to public TRON application programming interfaces (APIs) to retrieve these transaction records, extract cryptographic keys or location pointers, and connect to secondary payload contracts hosted on platforms like BNB Smart Chain. By capitalizing on TRON's nominal transaction overhead, high processing throughput, and massive legitimate transaction volume, adversaries create an unseizable setup that forces defenders to attempt simultaneous disruptions across distinct, decentralized ecosystems to break command access.

Adoption of the Solana Memo transaction

On the Solana network, transactions and the Solana Program Library (SPL) memo program operate under a distinct execution model compared to EVM-based smart contracts. A Solana transaction is an atomic package containing one or more instructions executed in sequence, capable of invoking multiple independent on-chain programs within a single block confirmation. The SPL Memo Program is a native, pre-deployed utility program residing directly within the Solana runtime. Rather than managing complex state machines or maintaining custom variables, the Memo Program simply validates an arbitrary string passed to it such as UTF-8 text or Base64-encoded binary data and records it directly into the transaction’s verified execution log.

Threat actors repurpose this architecture by treating the Memo Program as a lightweight, transaction-level dead drop resolver. In this technique, the actor controls standard Solana wallets and periodically broadcasts micro-value transactions that execute a call to the Memo Program. These transactions contain encrypted C2 IP addresses or staging domains. The implanted malware on the compromised endpoints is, configured with the Solana memo program ID, query public Solana JSON-RPC endpoints using standard calls like getSignaturesForAddress and getTransaction. The malware pulls the newest confirmed transaction associated with that wallet, extracts the payload from the memo instruction logs, decrypts the destination in memory, and initiates network beacons. When an operational IP or domain is sinkholed by security teams, the attacker simply broadcasts a new transaction with an updated memo payload, and the malware automatically retrieves the latest transaction on its next polling cycle without requiring binary updates on the victim machine.

Solana’s technical profile presents distinct characteristics compared to earlier public blockchains when evaluated as a low-latency, resilient data distribution layer. Processing over 65,000 transactions per second with sub-second block confirmation times around 0.4 seconds, the network enables near-instant propagation of broadcast data globally, avoiding the prolonged mempool delays characteristic of Bitcoin’s seven transactions per second (TPS) or Ethereum’s 15 – 30 TPS baseline. Economically, execution fees averaging approximately U.S. $0.000025 per transaction allow several updates to be published.

Threat actors are leveraging Solana memo transactions for hosting the C2 configurations that were first seen employed by the Lazarus APT group reported in March 2026. In September 2026, Cisco Talos discovered malicious activity conducted by a suspicious North Korea-aligned threat actor UAT-12643, including the use of the Overlord RAT and implementation of a resilient C2 server discovery mechanism by using the Solana blockchain. The actor embeds encrypted C2 URLs into the Solana blockchain using the Solana Memo Program, a native Solana program that validates and permanently records arbitrary text strings in the blockchain ledger as part of a transaction.

Looking ahead at defensive approach to counter bulletproof blockchain dead drops

The weaponization of public blockchains ranging from legacy Bitcoin script hashes to EVM smart contracts, TRON accounts, and Solana memo fields fundamentally inverts how we counter adversary infrastructure. By turning decentralized ledgers into resilient dead drop resolvers, threat actors have removed the single points of failure that security teams traditionally rely on to dismantle operations. Standard approaches like registrar-level domain seizures, hosting takedowns, and DNS sinkholing simply don't work when the staging record lives across many immutable nodes.

Enterprise defense needs to move past static indicators and focus on how endpoints interact with Web3 infrastructure. Because, resolving these dead drops relies on standard read-only Remote Procedure Call (RPC) queries, monitoring or blocking outbound traffic to public node providers like Infura, QuickNode, Tatum, and native chain endpoints could help reduce the attack surface significantly, if they aren’t required for business operations. Security teams should baseline normal developer or business activity and flag automated, high-frequency calls using methods like eth_call, getTransaction, and getSignaturesForAddress. Network defenders should inspect JSON-RPC payloads for anomalous base-encoded data and unexpected payload lengths. Also, endpoint telemetry should prioritize detecting lightweight in-memory decrypters before they can unpack and beacon out to the resolved C2 destinations.

As defenders mature these detection capabilities, adversary tradecraft will inevitably shift. Talos researchers are anticipating that on-chain C2 pipelines will move towards multi-chain fallback architectures, chaining lookups across multiple cryptocurrency networks to evade single-ecosystem blocks. As commercial RPC gateways implement stricter abuse detections, attackers will likely route the RPC lookups through decentralized RPC aggregators, private transaction relayers, or zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) verification systems that obscure the querying host. Eventually, tracking this activity requires treating public ledgers not just as financial tracks, but as an active adversary communications layer.

Title: UAT-12643: Suspected North Korea-aligned actor blends blockchain resilience with targeted infostealing
Context: Cisco Talos discovered malicious infrastructure associated with a financially motivated threat group we are tracking as UAT-12643
Full Text:
Cisco Talos discovered malicious infrastructure associated with a financially motivated threat group we are tracking as UAT-12643.

The actor’s arsenal has several payloads including the Go-based Overlord remote access trojan (RAT), a Python-based infostealer internally labelled “Good Game,” and a multi-cryptocurrency clipboard hijacker.

The threat actor is likely operating a campaign targeting cryptocurrency holders, gaming platform account owners, and VoIP software users based on the lure file names of the initial vectors and the payloads.

The Overlord RAT implements a command-and-control (C2) resilience technique in which encrypted server URLs are embedded in Solana blockchain transaction memos.

Victimology

The threat actor is potentially targeting victims in Europe, according to the payload’s keyword-based file harvesting capability, which specifically targeted documents that had file names in English, French, Spanish, and Portuguese.

Based on the lure themes and payload file names, the potential victim pool spans across multiple verticals. A lure financial statement decoy PDF — launched when the Good Game stealer is executed — indicates targeting finance and accounting staff. The Viber trojanized installer lure targets messaging platform users, while additional payload variants of files named microsip indicate targeting VoIP softphone operators, consistent with call-center or business telephone environments. Cryptocurrency and gaming users are also targeted by both the clipboard hijacker and the infostealer.

Potential links to North Korea-aligned actors

Talos assesses with low confidence that UAT-12643 is a North Korea-aligned advanced persistent threat (APT) actor based on overlaps in tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) with those of the other known North Korean APT actors.

In the current campaign, Talos observed that the actor is using the Overlord RAT as one of their payloads. The threat cluster called UNK_DeadDrop, likely a North Korean threat actor, had employed the Overlord RAT in their earlier campaigns as reported by the security researchers in June 2026.

The Overlord RAT variant observed in this campaign implements a blockchain C2 resilience technique with Solana blockchain transactions. This technique was first reported in March 2026, employed by the Lazarus APT group. Although the implementation methodology differs (earlier, it was through Node.js), the technique of leveraging Solana transaction memo stayed consistent.

Talos is aware that Overlord RAT and Solana blockchain hosting technique is also leveraged by other threat actors in their campaigns, as reported by external security researchers in October 2026.

Threat actor infrastructure

Talos observed that the actor hosted the malicious files on a server with IP address “41[.]216[.]188[.]11”, running a Flask-based file delivery service on port 8000 with resumable byte-range download support, and serving the payload staging directory. Due to the actor’s operational security failure, the server’s root folder was exposed to the internet, and Talos’ analysis of the exposed folder showed us actor’s tool sets, and the port numbers configured on the C2 server for different services.
